Since the blocked/parallel algorithm will differ bitwise from the sequential hash but the task specifies equivalent semantics with numerical tolerance validation, I'm leaning toward going with blocked/parallel and noting the hash mismatch is expected while reconstruction error stays within tolerance — though I'm still weighing whether that's the right call.\n\nActually, wait — a wavefront approach over anti-diagonals could preserve bit-exact ordering: each element's dependency chain and accumulation order stays identical to sequential, just computed level by level. With n=512, that gives around 1024 levels each with up to ~256 independent elements, and total work around n³/3 operations, so I'm estimating the sequential cost would be roughly 30-50ms plus a few milliseconds of barrier overhead across levels.\n\nSince the accumulation chains are inherently latency-bound and serial, the bitwise-preserving version can't exploit SIMD — speedup would come purely from running many independent chains across threads. Given the user wants \"equivalent semantics\" rather than strict bit-identical results, I'm leaning toward a blocked, SIMD-friendly implementation that trades exact reproducibility for much higher throughput, while noting that the numerical hash would change.\n\nHowever, the external validator likely compares hashes against a sequential reference run, so reordering could break validation — that's a real risk worth flagging. A middle ground would be a wavefront-style parallelization that preserves bit-exact sums while still scaling with available cores, though its parallelism is capped by the diagonal width at each level rather than the full thread count.\n\nThinking about the row dependencies more: each row's elements form a strictly sequential dot product, but rows can pipeline against each other using point-to-point progress tracking, where row i's column j only needs row j to have completed through its own diagonal.\n\nAssigning rows ascending with dynamic scheduling avoids deadlock, since a row's dependencies are always lower-numbered rows that started earlier, and progress can be tracked with atomic counters and acquire/release semantics for correctness while keeping bit-identical results to sequential execution.\n\nThe doacross approach avoids the barrier overhead of wavefront scheduling since rows run continuously rather than syncing at each diagonal level, and row-major storage keeps memory access contiguous for cache efficiency — both methods give identical numerical results, so I'm weighing which offers better practical performance.\n\nGiven the requirements stress both maximum performance and bitwise-equivalent semantics, the deterministic result is a strong point in favor since it keeps hash verification stable, though raw throughput still leans toward blocked approaches. I'm estimating the total FMA operation count for the triangular solve at roughly n³/6, which comes to about 22M operations for n=512, and now I need to check whether GCC's default floating-point contraction settings with -march=native will actually fuse these into FMA instructions given the project's C++20 configuration.\n\nI'm working out that the critical path through the diagonal elements is actually quite short—around 524k cycles or roughly 0.2ms for n=512—meaning a bit-exact parallel approach could realistically hit 8-30x speedup over the latency-bound sequential baseline of about 30ms, while a blocked approach might only get the sequential time down to 2-5ms before parallelizing.\n\nI'm also considering whether SIMD could help within the doacross scheme by processing multiple rows' dot products in parallel lanes, but that would require strided gather loads which tend to be slow, so I'm deciding to keep the design simpler and just go with bit-exact row-pipelined doacross, acknowledging the tradeoff between strict reproducibility and maximum raw performance.\n\nNow I'm sketching the atomic-based synchronization: tracking per-row completion with an atomic counter array so row i's update at column j can wait until row j's diagonal element is finalized, since that dependency is what makes naive parallel-for over rows incorrect.\n\nRow i only needs row j's columns 0..j, so row j's upper-triangle zeroing (columns > j) never conflicts with row i's reads — the dependency is race-free. I should also check for false sharing concerns between threads.\n\nFor diagonal failures, I need to add an abort flag: when a row detects a singular pivot, it sets a shared failed state, and any row spinning on another row's readiness must check that flag and break out too, so the whole computation can return false without deadlocking.\n\nActually, thinking through the dependency structure more carefully, since row j' depends on all earlier rows being ready, only the smallest failing diagonal can ever actually be reached—any later row would be stuck waiting on the failed row anyway, so at most one true failure point is ever hit.\n\nSo row j's computation at column c for c ≥ j' already depends on ready[j'] being set, meaning row j can't get ahead of row j' being marked ready before reaching that point.\n\nThis means failures are naturally sequential: the first failure detected corresponds to the smallest index, since a row can't fail at its own diagonal unless every earlier row's diagonal has already succeeded.\n\nSo instead of printing inside the parallel loop, I can track the minimum failing index using an atomic compare-exchange, then print the failure message once after the parallel region completes, before returning false. I need to make sure the NaN/non-positive check uses val <= 0 for safety.\n\nNow I'm working through how to handle early termination for the waiter threads once an abort signal is set — since an OpenMP for loop can't just `return` mid-iteration, I need each row's spin-wait to check the abort flag and skip remaining work via a local flag rather than breaking the loop directly.\n\nStill writing diagonal logic...\n\nSince row i' reads row i only at columns ≤ i, zeroing the upper part afterward doesn't conflict. I'm confirming the diagonal and off-diagonal sums match the original formula exactly, since multiplication order doesn't matter here.\n\nI'm also considering whether floating-point contraction (fma) behaves identically between the two versions under the same compiler flags — since the expression structure is identical, it should produce bitwise identical results, which I'll verify against the original binary's hash.\n\nOn the spin-wait question, I'm reasoning through deadlock safety: with dynamic scheduling of rows in increasing order, any thread holding row i has already seen all rows below it claimed by threads actively working, so progress is guaranteed regardless of oversubscription, though yielding occasionally would still help avoid starvation.\n\nFor the ready-flags vector, I need to be careful that a vector of atomics is properly zero-initialized since atomics aren't copyable — I'll explicitly loop to store zero rather than relying on implicit value-initialization, and I'm also considering padding each atomic to its own cache line to prevent false sharing between threads writing adjacent rows.\n\nThinking through the memory traffic pattern: since each row reads all previous rows' data from potentially different cores' caches, there's real cross-core traffic proportional to n^3/6, though for n=512 the whole matrix should still fit comfortably in L3. With 256 threads pipelining across 512 rows, I'm not sure yet if the dependency chain creates enough lag to hurt throughput — I'll need to actually benchmark this rather than reason it out further. I should also check the other parallelized sections, like the positive-definite matrix generation and validation steps.\n\nFor reductions on max error and relative error, max operations are order-independent so bitwise identical results should hold regardless of thread scheduling. The random matrix B generation stays sequential since it's only O(n^2) and trivial compared to the decomposition cost, and the diagonal dominance adjustment also stays as-is. I'm now setting up the atomic-based synchronization primitives needed for the waiter abort mechanism, including the failure flag and the wait function that spins on the row-ready counters.\n\nWriting synchronization logic...\n\nI'm making sure only one thread records the failing index using atomic exchange so there's no race if a failure check could theoretically trigger in multiple places, with the implicit barrier at the end of the parallel region guaranteeing visibility to the main thread. I also want to confirm the n==0 edge case works cleanly with empty vectors and loops that naturally become no-ops.\n\nFor scheduling, dynamic assignment makes sense since row i's workload grows roughly quadratically with i, so dynamic,1 balances load better than static given rows progress in a pipeline-like dependency pattern through the diagonal.\n\nFor the CMake setup, I'm adding OpenMP::OpenMP_CXX as a linked target alongside the existing math library, keeping the same style of linking while letting the imported target handle the compiler and linker flags automatically.\n\nSince I'm not calling any OpenMP runtime functions directly, I can skip including omp.h and just rely on the pragma directives, which get activated once -fopenmp is passed via the CMake target.\n\nBefore making changes, I want to establish a baseline by copying the original source and its common dependencies into the allowed temp directory, building it there, and comparing hashes and timing against my modified version.\n\n","time":{"start":1792981338340,"end":1792981384880},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

Every element is computed with exactly\n//   the same arithmetic, in the same order, as the sequential algorithm, so\n//   results are bit-for-bit identical to the sequential version.\n\nnamespace {\n\n// Spin (with yield back-off) until the progress counter reaches `target`.\n// Returns false if another row has already failed, so the caller can bail out.\ninline bool waitForRow(const std::atomic<size_t>& progress, const size_t target,\n                       const std::atomic<bool>& failed) {\n    unsigned spins = 0;\n    while (progress.load(std::memory_order_acquire) < target) {\n        if (failed.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {\n            return false;\n        }\n        if (++spins >= 256) {\n            std::this_thread::yield();\n            spins = 0;\n        }\n    }\n    return true;\n}\n\n}  // namespace\n\nbool choleskyDecomposition(std::vector<double>& A, const size_t n) {\n    // A is stored in row-major order.
